summary: Federated identity has mostly been used for network access and the web, with few common building blocks. This informational RFC describes the ABFAB architecture, which extends common security mechanisms so federated authentication can work for both web and non-web applications.

eli5.summary: One login card that works at many places, even for things that are not websites. This describes how the parts fit together.

questions: federated access beyond the web architecture
subtitle: Single sign-on for non-web applications using federated identity

tldr.problem: Federated identity systems like SAML work well for the web and for network access, but non-web applications lack a common framework to use federated authentication at scale.
tldr.mechanism: ABFAB extends standard protocols—GSS-API, EAP, RADIUS, and SAML—to enable federated access for non-web services, letting users sign in once and access many applications across organizations.
tldr.outcome: Non-web applications can now offer federated access with a single login credential, simplifying user experience and delegating identity management to organizations that already know the user.

facts.value: MSK (Master Session Key) and optionally EMSK

today: RFC 7831 is an Informational RFC describing the ABFAB architecture for non-web federated access. It has not been obsoleted and remains a reference for implementing federated authentication in email, conferencing, SSH, and other non-web services. The architecture is actively deployed in research networks and starting to expand to enterprise use.

sections.title: The Federation Problem for Non-Web Applications
sections.content:
Federated identity is common on the web (think single sign-on at colleges) and in network access (like institutional WiFi). But most non-web applications—email servers, video conferencing, research databases—do not have a standard way to accept federated credentials. Each one typically requires its own username and password.

This RFC describes ABFAB (Application Bridging for Federated Access Beyond Web), which extends proven security protocols to solve this. The architecture has three main players: a client (the user's software), a relying party (the application or service), and an identity provider (the organization that knows the user). The user authenticates once to their identity provider; the identity provider vouches for them to any number of relying parties.
sections.eli5: Instead of each app asking for a password, one trusted place confirms who you are, and you can access any participating app.

sections.title: Key Concepts and Federation Model
sections.content:
A federation is an agreement between identity providers and relying parties that defines how they work together. It sets out operational specs (which protocols, which authentication strength) and legal rules (what each party is responsible for, who covers costs).

The architecture uses a Network Access Identifier (NAI)—essentially a username@realm pair—as the user's name in the system. The realm part identifies the user's organization and its identity provider. When a user tries to access a service, the service first learns the NAI, then discovers the right identity provider and asks it to authenticate and vouch for the user.

The RFC emphasizes that federation does not require an advance relationship between the user and the service. The federation agreement between their organizations is enough—the two parties can meet for the first time when the user tries to access the service.
sections.eli5: Your realm (school or company) is like your postal code. When you give it, services can find your organization and ask it "Is this person yours?"

sections.title: The ABFAB Architecture and Data Flow
sections.content:
The ABFAB architecture has three communication channels. First, the client talks to the relying party using the application protocol (email, HTTP, SSH, etc.) layered over GSS-API, which abstracts the authentication. Second, the client and identity provider communicate by EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) methods, which is the strongest point of the design. Third, the relying party and identity provider use the AAA framework (RADIUS or Diameter) to route authentication and exchange attributes.

When a user tries to access a service: (1) the client sends its NAI to the relying party; (2) the relying party discovers the identity provider using the realm; (3) the relying party routes an EAP request to the identity provider via RADIUS; (4) the client and identity provider run an EAP authentication method to prove identity; (5) the identity provider checks policy and sends back cryptographic proof and, optionally, SAML assertions with attributes; (6) the relying party grants or denies access.
sections.eli5: You tell the service your realm. It looks up your school. Your school checks who you are using a secret method. Then the school tells the service "yes, it's them" or "no, it's not."

sections.title: Design Goals and Mechanisms
sections.content:
ABFAB aims to reuse existing standards rather than invent new ones. It builds on GSS-API and SASL (used in many non-web applications), EAP (the standard for access authentication), RADIUS and Diameter (deployed across the internet for access management), and SAML (the standard for federated attributes).

A crucial mechanism is channel binding, which prevents man-in-the-middle attacks by having both the client and the identity provider prove they know something about the communication channel—for example, by including a cryptographic hash of the TLS connection between client and relying party. This ensures that the identity provider is authenticating the right service and that the client is talking to the right service.
sections.eli5: Instead of inventing a new way to say "who are you," ABFAB uses proven methods from network access, web login, and email—just arranged in a new way.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC includes detailed security and privacy sections. The architecture protects the user's real identity from the relying party (only the identity provider knows it); the relying party sees only claims from the identity provider and attributes such as "student" or "faculty" rather than a name.

Privacy risks include tracking: organizations could use the realm identifier to track a user across multiple services. The RFC recommends that systems allow pseudonymous access where possible—for example, a service might not need a user's real name, just proof they are a student. When the identity provider releases attributes, it should do so according to policy and, ideally, with user awareness or control.

The architecture also inherits security properties from its building blocks (EAP's mutual authentication, RADIUS's integrity protection) while adding channel binding to prevent proxy attacks.
sections.eli5: Services see what you did, not who you are. You could be "a student" without your school revealing your name. But if you use your real email, they can tell it's you.

sections.title: Deployment and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
ABFAB is designed to scale to large federations with many identity providers and relying parties. The AAA routing infrastructure already supports this—intermediaries (AAA proxies, federation brokers) can route messages between organizations without every pair needing a direct connection.

A notable large-scale example is eduroam, which uses RADIUS to provide Wi-Fi access across universities worldwide. ABFAB builds on this infrastructure, so many organizations can add application-level support without new network infrastructure.

The RFC notes that both RADIUS and Diameter can be used, though RADIUS is more widely deployed today in enterprise and university networks, while Diameter is common in mobile networks. Future documents may standardize the same attributes for Diameter. Proxies that convert between the two already exist, so mixed deployments are possible.
sections.eli5: A school in one country can work with a service in another without them knowing each other beforehand. The federation network passes messages between them, like the postal system.
